newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta Labour's Sant to step back from Europe.
newsitem.headline: Malta Labour's Sant to step back from Europe.

text.p: Fast-talking and fast-moving, Labour Party leader Alfred Sant, who claimed victory in Malta's general elections, is a fervent believer in neutrality for the small Mediterranean island state.
He promised that a Labour government would abandon Malta's application to join the European Union and would immediately pull out of NATO's Partnership for Peace programme.

"We should have a special relationship (with the EU), not membership," he said in an interview with Reuters. "I would like to see security, not military, cooperation, for example on drugs, contraband and the movement of people."
Sant's Labour Party said it won Saturday's elections, ousting the Nationalist Party of Edward Fenech Adami, which had a three-seat majority in the outgoing 65-member parliament.
Ironically, Sant, 48, has worked more closely with Europe than most Maltese, serving as second and then first secretary at the Malta mission to the European Communities in Brussels from 1970 to 1975.

Ten years later he was an adviser to the prime minister, a job which included negotiations on relations with the Council of Europe and the then European Community. He is fluent in English, French and Italian and reads German.

Even Sant's critics accept that he has transformed the Labour Party, increasing its appeal to the political middle ground and giving it a modern image. It has built its own headquarters and it is alone in having its own television station.
A physicist by training, Sant studied public administration in France, then business studies in the United States, gaining his doctorate at Harvard Business School.
In the 1980s he was chairman of a joint venture with Libyan and Algerian interests, a position in tune with his view that Malta should have ties to nations along the south Mediterranean coast.
Sant disagrees with the idea of Malta becoming a "bridge" between Europe and North Africa but he says he could envisage it as a "frontier post".

"We want a special relationship with Europe but I argue that you start with your neighbours," he said, adding that he wanted good relations with Libya although Malta would adhere to U.N. sanctions imposed on Tripoli for the Lockerbie aircraft bombing.
Sant was elected president of the Labour Party in 1984 and took over its leadership in 1992.
His marriage was annulled by the court and he has a daughter, Marta, 11. He has written three novels, short stories and plays -- all in the Maltese language.
